title: Design clients paying late invoices: causes and fixes for Mac designers in 2026
metaTitle: Design clients paying late invoices: fixes for designers
description: Why design clients pay late, what it costs you, and free fixes that work: payment terms, a chase schedule and reminders on your Mac.
secondaryKeywords: how to get paid on time as a designer
intro: Design clients paying late invoices is a common problem, and most of it is fixable. The fix is written payment terms, a chase schedule you follow every time, and automatic reminders where your invoicing tool offers them. Bonsai's data found 28% of designers' invoices were paid at least a day late. This page covers what late payment costs, why it happens, and fixes you can use today without buying anything.
tldr: Bonsai's data puts designers' late invoices at 28%, close to the 29% rate for all freelancers in its sample.
Late payment costs cash, chasing time, unpaid work and sometimes clients you stop taking on.
Most late payment comes from unclear terms, slow approval and forgetfulness rather than refusal.
Write terms, define when work is done, and chase in three steps: reminder, formal notice, final demand.

blocks.text: Late payment is a cash problem before it is anything else. You finish a logo system or a website redesign, send the invoice, and then wait. Rent, software and tax keep their own schedule. Many freelancers cover that gap from savings or a credit card. A few late invoices can stall a whole month.
What late payment costs a design freelancer

The cost shows up in four places. It is cash you cannot spend yet. It is hours spent chasing. It is work you never get paid for. It is clients you stop taking on. Each one is easy to dismiss alone. Together they change how you price and how you plan your year.

Read these numbers with their sources in mind. Bonsai analysed three years of invoices from more than 100,000 freelancers. It found 29% of invoices were paid at least a day late. In that data, designers were paid late 28% of the time. Software developers were late 29% of the time, so designers are not an outlier.

The UK figures cover more freelancers. IPSE reports that 54% of freelancers have had a client delay a payment during their self-employed career. It also reports that 31% have completed work and never been paid for it. Freelancers who had been paid late were owed an average of £5,230.
How much time chasing invoices takes

The UK Small Business Commissioner found that businesses affected by late payment spend an average of 86 hours a year chasing it. That figure covers all businesses, not designers alone. For a studio of one, those hours are unbilled. They come out of design time and marketing time.

The same research says 15% of surveyed businesses have avoided doing business with specific customers because of their payment behaviour. That is the cost most designers feel last, and it lasts longest. A client who pays slowly today may not come back with a second project.

blocks.text: Why design clients pay late

Clients rarely decide to skip a designer. IPSE lists four common causes. The first is cash flow. The client delays spending because their own customers have not paid them. The other three are unclear terms, internal bureaucracy and simple forgetfulness.

items: Cash flow: the client holds money until their own customers pay.
Unclear terms: nobody agreed when payment is due, so nobody feels late.
Internal bureaucracy: the invoice sits in a shared inbox or never reaches finance.
Forgetfulness: the approver meant to forward it and did not.

blocks.text: Deliberate refusal is described as the least common cause. That changes how you respond. A lost invoice needs a clean resend, not a sharp email. A cash-flow delay needs a clear date you can both agree to. Refusal needs a paper trail and a formal notice.

Bonsai's data points to two patterns worth watching. Invoices over $20,000 were about three times as likely to be paid late as invoices under $100. Crypto payments were late almost three times as often as ACH or bank transfers. These are correlations in one dataset, not proof of cause. They still tell you where to tighten terms first.
Fix one: write payment terms nobody can misread

Put the payment terms in the proposal and again on the invoice. Say when payment is due in plain words. The date printed on the invoice works. So does a set number of days from the invoice date, written out in full. Avoid vague triggers such as 'on completion' unless you define completion.
If you share proposals as a Figma file or a Canva doc, put the same line on the first page. Finance teams often see only the first page. Put the payment line there, not buried on page six.
A common mistake is putting terms only in an email reply. That reply gets buried in a long thread. Put the terms in the signed contract, then repeat them in the invoice footer. Two places beat one.
Fix two: define when the work counts as done

IPSE recommends that you define when work counts as complete. Pick one trigger: submission, acknowledgement or acceptance. Many design jobs stall because nobody agreed what finished means. The client asks for one more round, then another, and the invoice waits with them.

Make the trigger concrete. For a Figma deliverable, the invoice goes out when you share the final file link. Acceptance can be a written approval in a comment, or a Slack message from the named contact. Save that message in the project. A phone call leaves no record.
Fix three: send the invoice to the person who pays

Slow approval is one of the most common causes. The invoice goes to a design lead who has no access to payments, and it sits there. Ask at kickoff who approves invoices and who processes payment. Then send the invoice to both, with the approver named in the first line.

items: Ask for the accounts payable address, if the client has one.
Ask whether they need a purchase order number, and add it to the invoice.
Ask how often finance runs payments, so you can time the invoice.
Keep the approver copied on every chaser.

blocks.text: Fix four: a chase schedule you follow every time

IPSE suggests a three-step process. Send a gentle reminder first. After a week, send a formal notice that refers to the invoice and the contract terms. After two weeks, send a final demand. Use the same steps for every client, so the process reads as routine, not personal.

rows: The day after the due date
Invoice number, amount, due date, a payment link and thanks
Refers to the invoice and contract payment terms, and asks for a payment date
States the amount, the next step and the date you will take it
blocks.caption: Chase stages based on IPSE's three-step advice. Adjust the tone to the client.

blocks.text: Send each chaser from the same email thread. The history stays in one place, and finance can see the earlier messages. Keep each message short. A chaser should read like a receipt, not a complaint. Attach the invoice every time.
Set up automatic reminders in your invoicing tool

Automatic reminders take the awkwardness out of chasing. They fix forgetfulness, which IPSE lists as a common cause. Most invoicing tools have them. Each one has its own rules, so check the settings before you trust them.

items: QuickBooks Online: Settings > Account and settings > Sales > Reminders > Edit. You can schedule reminders up to 90 days before or after the due date.
QuickBooks Desktop: Edit > Preferences > Payments > Company Preferences for the switch, then Customers > Payment Reminders > Schedule Payment Reminders.
Stripe: automatic invoice advancement is on by default for invoices created in the Dashboard. Turn it off for one invoice from its overflow menu.
FreshBooks: an Invoice is Overdue notification tells you when a client is late and prompts you to enable late reminders.
Xero: check Xero's help centre for its reminder settings and limits before you rely on them.

blocks.title: Reminders only cover what they can see
blocks.text: QuickBooks Online only sends automatic reminders for unpaid invoices emailed from QuickBooks that match your settings. An invoice sent as a PDF from another app gets no reminder. Check how each invoice was sent before you assume a reminder went out.

No study checked here shows that automatic reminders cut late payment for designers specifically. Use them as a backstop. Your own schedule, with the same steps every time, still does most of the work.
Statutory interest for UK business invoices

If your clients are UK businesses, the law gives you more than a polite reminder. The Late Payment of Commercial Debts (Interest) Act 1998 already allows statutory interest of 8% above Bank of England base rate on late business invoices. Adfin's worked example, with base rate at 3.75%, comes to 11.75% a year.

The clock does not always start on the invoice date. Section 4 of the Act defines the relevant 60-day period. It starts on the later of two days: the day you performed your obligation, and the day the client had notice of the debt. Check that wording before you quote a date.

Adfin also lists fixed compensation of £40, £70 or £100 per invoice. That detail comes from a secondary source, so check the Act before you quote it. Keep any figure to a formal notice, not a casual email.

Reform is still moving. Adfin says the proposed Commercial Payments Bill would cap payment terms at 60 days for large businesses paying smaller suppliers. It would also make statutory interest compulsory. As of Adfin's 22 October 2026 note, none of that is law.

blocks.title: Interest is a right, not a threat
blocks.text: Statutory interest is part of UK law, but it is not something to wave at a client. Use it only in a formal notice. Get advice if the amount is large or the client disputes the work.
Worked example: one invoice, three messages

Say you delivered a brand identity to a client whose finance team processes payments. The invoice went out on delivery, with the due date printed on it. On the day after the due date, you send a gentle reminder in the original thread. Nothing comes back.

A week later, you send the formal notice. It names the invoice, quotes the payment clause from the contract, and asks for a payment date. If that date passes, you send the final demand two weeks after the due date. It states the amount, the next step and the day you will take it.

Keep the promise you make in the final demand. If you said you would pause work, pause it, and tell the client the day you did. Lazur can help draft these three messages in plain language. You still read them, change them and send them yourself.
Mistakes that make late payment worse

items: Chasing only in chat. A Slack message gets lost. Send chasers by email with the invoice attached.
Apologising for asking. Say 'I am following up on invoice' and stop there.
Starting the next phase before the last invoice is paid. Pause new work, or ask for a deposit.
Waiting months before the first reminder. Send the reminder the day after the due date.
Discounting to get paid. A discount teaches the client that late is fine.
Leaving out the invoice number. Without it, finance cannot match the payment.

blocks.text: Edge cases: regulated clients and confidential work

Most design clients are businesses with no special data rules. Some are not. A healthcare provider, a law firm or a bank may restrict what you share with outside tools. Follow their rules on client and patient data before you paste a file, a screenshot or a case detail into any app. That includes AI assistants.

Confidentiality clauses matter too. An NDA can cover briefs, mockups and invoice details. Read the contract before you ask an AI tool to rewrite a chaser that names the project. If your client or employer has a data policy, their policy wins. Ask them what is allowed.
Where Lazur helps, and where it does not

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac. Hold ⌥⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. Ask where a control is, and Lazur draws a circle and label around it. Ask how to do something, and Lazur guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click.

For late payments, that means three real uses. Ask Lazur to walk you through the reminder settings in your invoicing tool. Ask it to draft a chaser, then read the draft aloud. Hold fn to dictate the final text at the cursor in Mail or any other app.

Lazur does not click buttons, send email or log into your invoicing tool for you. It does not operate other apps. The sending, the approval and the choice to chase stay with you. That keeps every message and every decision in your hands.
A chase routine that fits your Mac

A routine works best where you already work. Put each due date in Apple Reminders or Calendar. Set the chase dates on the same day you send the invoice. Send chasers from Mail, so the thread stays in one place. Store the invoice PDF in the same folder as the project files.

Dictation helps when you are tired of writing the same message. Hold fn to dictate clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app. Dictation is unlimited on both Lazur plans, so you can use it for every chaser you send.
What to do next

Start with the client who owes you money now. If the due date has passed, send the gentle reminder today. Then write payment terms into your next proposal and set the chase dates before you start the work. Check your invoicing tool's reminder settings once, and keep them on.

faq.question: How common is late payment for designers?
faq.answer: Bonsai's data, from more than 100,000 freelancers over three years, found designers were paid late 28% of the time. Software developers were at 29%. Those numbers come from one platform's invoices, so treat them as a guide, not a census of the whole industry.

faq.question: Can I charge interest on a late invoice?
faq.answer: In the UK, the Late Payment of Commercial Debts (Interest) Act 1998 allows statutory interest of 8% above Bank of England base rate on late business invoices. Check the Act and get advice before you quote it, especially if the client disputes the work.

faq.question: What should a first reminder say?
faq.answer: Keep it to the invoice number, the amount, the due date and a way to pay. Thank the client. Skip the apology and the history. A reminder should read like a receipt, not an accusation.

faq.question: Should I stop work when an invoice is late?
faq.answer: Many designers pause new work until the last invoice is paid. Say so in the contract or in the final demand. Pausing is a business choice, so check your agreement before you act on it.

faq.question: Do automatic reminders work?
faq.answer: They help with forgetfulness, which is one common cause of late payment. No study checked for this page shows they cut late payment for designers. Use them as a backstop next to your own schedule.

faq.question: Does Lazur send the reminders for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur guides you, points at things, answers out loud and drafts text. It does not click buttons, send email or operate your invoicing tool. You send each message yourself.

faq.question: What if my client works in a regulated field?
faq.answer: Follow their rules on client or patient data. Do not paste files, screenshots or case details into any app, including AI assistants, unless their policy allows it. Ask them what is permitted before you start.

faq.question: Do the UK interest rules apply everywhere?
faq.answer: No. The statutory interest and 60-day rules on this page are UK law. Other countries have their own late payment rules. Check your local rules, or ask an adviser who knows the rules where your client is based.

problem: chasing late payments from design clients

costs.title: Cash you already earned
costs.text: Every late invoice is cash you cannot spend yet. You may cover rent, software and tax from savings or a credit card while the money sits with the client. For a studio of one, one large late invoice can decide whether the next month feels comfortable or tight.

costs.title: Hours spent chasing
costs.text: The UK Small Business Commissioner found businesses affected by late payment spend an average of 86 hours a year chasing it. Those hours are rarely billed. Emails, calls and follow-ups take time away from the design work you would otherwise sell.

costs.title: Work you never get paid for
costs.text: IPSE reports that 31% of freelancers have completed work and never been paid for it. The chance of collecting drops once a project closes and the file is handed over. Watch for the early signs, such as vague approvals and missed payment dates.

costs.title: Clients you stop taking
costs.text: The Commissioner reports that 15% of surveyed businesses have avoided doing business with specific customers because of how they pay. Designers who get burned often start asking for deposits, turning down slow clients, or taking less work from good ones.

causes.title: Cash flow on the client's side
causes.text: IPSE lists clients delaying spending for cash-flow reasons as a common cause. The client may hold your invoice because their own customers have not paid them. This is rarely personal, but it still lands on your bank balance.

causes.title: Unclear payment terms
causes.text: If nobody wrote down when payment is due, nobody is late. Clients read a missing date as a soft deadline. Vague triggers such as 'on completion' cause the same confusion, because completion means different things to each side.

causes.title: Invoices lost in approval
causes.text: Internal bureaucracy is on IPSE's list. The invoice lands in a shared inbox, waits for a manager, or never reaches the finance team. Slow routes add weeks without anyone deciding to pay late.

causes.title: Simple forgetfulness
causes.text: IPSE also lists forgetfulness. An approver meant to forward the invoice, got busy, and moved on. A reminder fixes this more often than a firm email does, because it arrives at the right moment.

causes.title: Your own silence
causes.text: Bonsai says some clients see freelancers as unable to enforce on-time payment. If you let the first late date pass with no reply, the client learns that lateness costs nothing. A quiet first reminder teaches the same lesson.

causes.title: Deliberate refusal, which is rare
causes.text: Deliberate refusal is described as the least common cause. When it does happen, the tone of your chaser matters less than your paper trail. Keep the contract, delivery records and approval messages together.

fixes.title: Write terms into the contract and invoice
fixes.text: Put the payment date in the proposal and repeat it in the invoice footer. Use plain words for the due date. Avoid vague triggers unless you define them in the same document. Two places beat one.

fixes.title: Define when work counts as done
fixes.text: IPSE suggests choosing a trigger: submission, acknowledgement or acceptance. Make the trigger concrete in your project notes. A written approval in a comment or an email is stronger than a phone call that nobody wrote down.

fixes.title: Send the invoice to the person who pays
fixes.text: Ask at kickoff who approves invoices and who runs payments. Put both names on the first invoice email. Ask for the accounts address and any purchase order number before you send anything.

fixes.title: Send a reminder the day after
fixes.text: Start with a gentle reminder the day after the due date. Keep it to the invoice number, the amount, the due date and a payment link. No apology, and no lecture about the last project.

fixes.title: Escalate on a fixed schedule
fixes.text: After a week, send a formal notice that refers to the invoice and the contract terms. After two weeks, send a final demand. Following the same steps every time makes your process look normal, not personal.

fixes.title: Turn on reminders where they exist
fixes.text: QuickBooks Online, QuickBooks Desktop, Stripe and FreshBooks all offer reminder features. Turn them on, then check each invoice was sent in a way the reminder can see. Treat reminders as a backstop, not the whole plan.

fixes.title: Use statutory interest only in a formal notice
fixes.text: UK business invoices already carry statutory interest of 8% above base rate under the 1998 Act. Mention it only in a formal notice. Check the Act or an adviser before you quote a figure, especially on a disputed invoice.

plan.label: Before send
plan.title: Write the terms into the contract
plan.text: Check the proposal and the invoice footer. Both should state when payment is due, in plain words. Ask who approves invoices, and get that name in writing before you start work.

plan.label: Due date
plan.title: Set the chase dates
plan.text: Add the due date to Apple Reminders or Calendar. Add a second reminder for the day after. You can ask Lazur to add these by voice if that is faster for you.

plan.label: Day after
plan.title: Send the gentle reminder
plan.text: Send one short email from the original thread. Include the invoice number, the amount, the due date and a payment link. Skip the apology and the history of the project.

plan.label: One week
plan.title: Send a formal notice
plan.text: Refer to the invoice and the contract payment terms. Ask for a payment date. Draft the notice with Lazur, read it aloud, then send it from your mail app.

plan.label: Two weeks
plan.title: Send the final demand
plan.text: State the amount, the next step and the date you will take it. Keep that date. If you said you would pause new work, pause it and say so in writing.

plan.label: Monthly
plan.title: Review open invoices
plan.text: Open QuickBooks Online or your invoicing tool and check every overdue invoice. Confirm the reminder settings still match your terms. Look for any invoice sent outside the tool.
